question: How to detect or extract pretraining data from language models? Are there related works on this topic?

ingredients.name: answer_critical_0
ingredients.criterion: Defines the core task: given a piece of text and black-box access to an LLM whose pretraining data is undisclosed, determine whether the model was trained on that text.
examples: Given a text and an LLM whose training data is undisclosed, we ask: was this text seen during training?
The detection problem asks whether provided text appeared in the (undisclosed) pretraining data, with only black-box model access.

ingredients.name: answer_critical_1
ingredients.criterion: Describes MIN-K% PROB and its hypothesis: unseen examples tend to contain a few outlier tokens with very low probability under the LLM, while seen (memorized) examples are less likely to have such low-probability words; the method scores text by its lowest-probability k% of tokens.
examples: MIN-K% PROB identifies seen text by checking whether a small fraction of tokens have anomalously low likelihood under the model.
The method examines the lowest-probability k% of tokens to classify text as seen or unseen.

ingredients.name: answer_critical_2
ingredients.criterion: Notes that MIN-K% PROB requires no knowledge of the pretraining corpus and no additional training, unlike prior methods that required training a reference model on data similar to the pretraining set.
examples: Unlike earlier approaches that train a reference model on similar data, MIN-K% PROB needs neither corpus knowledge nor extra training.
Prior approaches needed a reference model trained on data similar to the pretraining set; MIN-K% PROB does not.

ingredients.name: answer_critical_3
ingredients.criterion: Mentions the WIKIMIA dynamic benchmark, which uses data created before versus after model training (e.g., Wikipedia revisions around the training cutoff) to provide gold-truth labels for evaluating detection.
examples: WIKIMIA uses Wikipedia revisions before and after the model's training cutoff as positive and negative examples.
They construct a dynamic benchmark with gold truth labels by using text that existed before versus after training.

ingredients.name: answer_critical_4
ingredients.criterion: Explains why detection matters: pretraining corpora at trillion-token scale almost certainly contain copyrighted materials, personally identifiable information, and leaked benchmark test data, yet training data is rarely disclosed.
examples: At trillions of tokens, pretraining data surely includes copyrighted text, PII, and leaked benchmark test sets, yet is rarely disclosed.
Since LLM training data is rarely disclosed, we need tools to know which problematic text is included.

ingredients.name: valuable_0
ingredients.criterion: Identifies WIMBD (What's In My Big Data?) as related work: a platform with sixteen count/search-based analyses at scale revealing and comparing the contents of large corpora such as C4, The Pile, and RedPajama (35+ TB across ten corpora).
examples: WIMBD uses count and search at scale to analyze over 35 terabytes and compare ten corpora like C4 and The Pile.
As related work, WIMBD reveals what is inside big training corpora through large-scale count and search.

ingredients.name: valuable_1
ingredients.criterion: Identifies Data Portraits as related work: data-sketching-based artifacts that record training data (e.g., for The Pile and The Stack) with only ~3% size overhead, enabling fast, space-efficient queries about whether an example was encountered during training, such as for test set leakage and model plagiarism.
examples: Data Portraits use data sketching with only 3% dataset-size overhead to record training data for downstream inspection.
Data Portraits document The Pile and The Stack, enabling queries about test set leakage and model plagiarism.

ingredients.name: valuable_2
ingredients.criterion: Cites specific findings from corpus analysis, such as benchmark contamination of the Winograd Schema Challenge and parts of GLUE and SuperGLUE, and high prevalence of duplicates, synthetic, low-quality, PII, and toxic content (e.g., ~50% duplicates in RedPajama and LAION-2B-en).
examples: WIMBD found contamination in benchmarks like the Winograd Schema Challenge and parts of GLUE/SuperGLUE.
About 50% of documents in RedPajama and LAION-2B-en are duplicates.
